scenes.heading: Equations with Fractions
scenes.subheading: Grade 8 Mathematics · Factorisation and equations, part 3
scenes.narration: Welcome to part three of our series on factorisation and equations. In this lesson we solve equations that contain fractions.

scenes.heading: The big idea
bullets: Fractions make an equation look hard
Multiply every term by the LCD to clear the fractions
scenes.narration: Fractions can make an equation look hard, but there is a simple trick. Multiply every term by the lowest common denominator, the L C D. The fractions disappear, and you solve the equation as usual.

scenes.heading: Example 1
scenes.narration: Solve x over three equals four. x is divided by three, so multiply both sides by three. x equals four times three, which is twelve.

scenes.heading: Example 2
scenes.narration: Solve x plus two, over five, equals three. Multiply both sides by five: x plus two equals fifteen. Subtract two: x equals thirteen.

scenes.heading: Example 3
scenes.narration: Solve two x over three, minus one, equals five. First add one to both sides: two x over three equals six. Multiply both sides by three: two x equals eighteen. Divide by two: x equals nine.

scenes.heading: Example 4: Two fractions
scenes.narration: Solve x over two, plus x over three, equals five. The LCD of two and three is six. Multiply every term by six, including the five on the right. Six times x over two is three x. Six times x over three is two x. Six times five is thirty. So five x equals thirty, and x equals six.

scenes.heading: Check your answer
scenes.narration: Let us check. Substitute x equals six into the left hand side: six over two, plus six over three, is three plus two, which is five. That equals the right hand side, so x equals six is correct.

scenes.heading: Tips
bullets: Multiply every term by the LCD, even terms without fractions
Put a top with two terms in brackets
Check by substituting into the original equation
scenes.narration: Three tips. Multiply every term by the LCD, even the terms without fractions. When the top of a fraction has two terms, put it in brackets before you multiply. And check by substituting your answer into the original equation.
